question: Are there any papers showing the effectiveness of quality filtering of LLM pre-training data using more advanced models such as BERT? I found many prior studies only use fasttext but it could make the filtering models pretty weak...

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer directly confirms that papers exist demonstrating the effectiveness of quality filtering with more advanced neural models (beyond fastText), citing at least FineWebEdu and Llama 3 as concrete examples.
examples: Yes — FineWebEdu and Llama 3 both use neural models for quality filtering and show effectiveness
Several state-of-the-art LMs have leveraged trained neural models as content classifiers

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer explains why the user encountered mostly fastText: it is widely used in existing pipelines (e.g., CCNet/Dolma for language identification, OpenWebMath for domain filtering), typically with simple linear classifiers or thresholds.
examples: Dolma's web pipeline uses CCNet's FastText language ID model, keeping pages with English score >= 0.5 (removing 61.7% by bytes)
OpenWebMath notes language filtering is often done with simple linear classifiers like fastText

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer presents GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) as another prior approach using a non-neural logistic regression classifier (Spark tokenizer/HashingTF features) trained on curated positives (WebText, Wikipedia, web books) vs. unfiltered Common Crawl negatives, with scores used to re-sample documents.
examples: GPT-3 trained a logistic regression classifier with WebText/Wikipedia/books as positives and unfiltered Common Crawl as negatives
GPT-3 re-sampled Common Crawl prioritizing documents the classifier predicted to be higher quality

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer describes FineWebEdu's methodology — a snowflake embedding model trained on ~410,000 FineWeb samples rated 0-5 for educational quality by Llama-3-70B-Instruct — and its ablation evidence: a 1.82B model trained on 350B FineWebEdu tokens outperforming other open web datasets on MMLU, ARC, and OpenBookQA.
examples: FineWebEdu trains a snowflake embedding model on 410,000 FineWeb samples scored 0-5 by Llama-3-70B-Instruct
A 1.82B model trained on 350B FineWebEdu tokens outperformed all other open web datasets on MMLU, ARC, and OpenBookQA

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: The answer details Llama 3's RoBERTa-based (Liu et al., 2019) classifier trained on synthetic labels generated by Llama 2's chat model judging whether cleaned web documents meet quality requirements.
examples: Llama 3 uses a RoBERTa-based classifier (Liu et al., 2019a)
Llama 2's chat model was instructed to judge whether cleaned web documents meet quality criteria, producing training labels

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer addresses the user's concern that fastText-based filtering may be weak, noting that fine-tuned pre-trained language models like BERT typically outperform fastText classifiers in general NLP tasks.
examples: Fine-tuning pre-trained LMs like BERT often shows much better performance than fastText-based classifiers
Simple fastText filters may not be precise enough to identify high-quality pre-training data

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer acknowledges that neural quality classifiers are much more computationally expensive than fastText or logistic regression, explaining why simple models remain prevalent at web scale.
examples: Neural quality classifiers are often much more computationally expensive than logistic regression approaches
Efficient non-neural models like fastText are chosen to manage computational costs when filtering trillion-token datasets

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer situates classifier-based filtering within the broader taxonomy of quality filtering: perplexity-based (KenLM 5-gram in CCNet), classifier-based (GPT-3, FineWebEdu, Llama 3), and rule-based (C4, MassiveWeb) approaches.
examples: CCNet uses a 5-gram Kneser-Ney KenLM language model to filter by perplexity
C4 and MassiveWeb use rule-based filters such as character counts, symbol proportions, and word length heuristics

ingredients.name: valuable_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer provides context on why quality filtering is needed for massive Common Crawl-scale pre-training corpora.
examples: Raw web data such as Common Crawl requires extensive processing and content filtering before pre-training
Filtering is a critical step in building high-quality pre-training datasets at web scale
